TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
TUESDAY, 18 AUGUST 2026
AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 9, DAY 2
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH TAMARA PHILLPS, COUNSEL
ASSISTING
AMY MUNRO SC WITH DR DAVID BLUMENTHAL, THE
COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA
SOPHIE CALLAN SC, THE STATE OF NEW SOUTH WALES
LEON ZWIER, VARIOUS JEWISH COMMUNAL BODIES

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you, Commissioner. Over the course of today and into
the first half of tomorrow, we will be hearing from witnesses who are engaged in
educational programming, in research and in other initiatives that are directed to advancing
social cohesion across various levels of the education system. The first witnesses today
will be Dr Daniel Heller and Dr Farid Zaid who are appearing via AVL.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<DR FARID ZAID, AFFIRMED VIA AVL
<DR DANIEL HELLER, SWORN VIA AVL
MR LANCASTER SC: Dr Heller, can I start with you. Could you state your full name,
please?
DR HELLER: Sure, Daniel Kupfert Heller.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are a Co-Director of Brave Conversations Project?
DR HELLER: I am indeed.
MR LANCASTER SC: You prepared a written statement dated 12 August 2026. Are the
contents of that statement true and correct?
DR HELLER: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. Commissioner the document is
STAT.8999.0033.0006. I tender the statement.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. The statement will be admitted.
MR LANCASTER SC: Dr Zaid, please state your full name.
DR ZAID: Farid Zaid.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are also a Co-Director of Brave Conversations Project?
DR ZAID: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have prepared a written statement dated 6 August 2026.
Are the contents of that statement true and correct?
DR ZAID: They are.

MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I tender Dr Zaid's statement.
STAT.8999.0033.0004.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Dr Zaid's statement will be received as an exhibit.
MR LANCASTER SC: And they each refer to and annex the submission made by Brave
Conversations Project and that's part of the tender.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In November 2024, you together launched the Brave
Conversations Project, of which you are co-directors, and I'll ask you about that very
shortly, but first just a little of your professional background. Dr Zaid, you are a cognitive
scientist at the Turner Institute of Brain and Mental Health, which is a research institute
attached to Monash University in Victoria?
DR ZAID: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are also a senior lecturer in Psychology at Monash and you
have held that position since 2018.
DR ZAID: Yes, correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are a Director of the Graduate Diploma of Psychology at
Monash; is that right?
DR ZAID: I've now become the Assistant Director. I've stepped down a little bit to focus
on Brave Conversations.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. You have an undergraduate degree in mathematics
and economics and an honours degree in psychology?
DR ZAID: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: In 2021, you completed a PhD in Moral Psychology?
DR ZAID: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: For those who don't know what that involves, could you explain
what moral psychology is?
DR ZAID: Moral Psychology is a field of research and study that focuses on the way
human beings reason about right and wrong, in a single sentence.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. But people obviously write PhDs about it.

DR ZAID: Sure, and books and lectures, yes. It's a nuanced, complicated field.
MR LANCASTER SC: And for those also who may not know, the field of cognitive
science, cognitive neuroscience, could you describe that in a sentence or two what they
involve?
DR ZAID: I emphasise the science part, even though I teach psychology, because I'm not
a registered psychologist, and it's a protected term in Australia, and so although I teach
future psychologists, I myself am not a registered one. And so I use the broader term of
"science". And cognitive just really means or refers to things to do with the mind and the
brain, when it comes to thinking and reasoning.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. And, Dr Heller, you are a senior lecturer at the
School of Historical, Philosophical and Indigenous Studies at Monash?
DR HELLER: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have a PhD in History from Stanford University?
DR HELLER: I do.
MR LANCASTER SC: What are your areas of academic and teaching specialisation,
please?
DR HELLER: Well, they are in Eastern European history, history of the Middle East,
both of those in the modern era so 19th and 20th century.
MR LANCASTER SC: In the submission that has been prepared and submitted, you've
observed that you have spent a career teaching Israeli and Palestinian history, not to flatten
it into slogans but help students sit with power, identity, trauma and responsibility and to
stay in the room when it gets hard. Can you give a sense of how, in your career as
a history educator, you have sought to facilitate students staying in the room without
flattening history into slogans, as you have described?
DR HELLER: The first piece of this puzzle is a deep sense of humility. So once
I received my PhD in history and I began teaching undergraduate students, I very quickly
realised I did not have the skillset as a university educator to be able to work with students
when they genuinely struggled to not only hear different views from classmates but even
read things that might challenge their perceptions of the world. So that humility led me to
pursue graduate studies in psychology and to bring back different tools from the world of
psychology into the classroom.
So I think that the number one thing I can say about cultivating an environment in
a classroom where students are open to listening across difference and to sitting in
discomfort is to model that behaviour. So modelling humility as an educator, I think
everything else flows from that, as well as building trust with the students and letting them

know that we care deeply about their learning journey. Everything else is commentary,
quite frankly.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. Dr Zaid, you have described the Brave
Conversations Project as one that facilitates discussion-based workshops, providing
participants with practical tools to engage in constructive disagreement. Can you describe
what prompted you to get involved in the development of this initiative in the lead-up to
November 2024 when it began?
DR ZAID: Absolutely. I guess, like Daniel, I just had personal experience in my
classrooms. I've been teaching for many years as a lecturer after obtaining my
qualifications, but certainly for many years even before as a sessional tutor and an assistant
lecturer and I found that, surprisingly - initially; I'm no longer surprised. But initially I
was deeply surprised by my students' inability to distinguish discomfort in the classroom,
which is necessary for learning, and distress. And I found that even through my short
career, that line between discomfort and distress became narrower and narrower as the
years passed and the polarisation in our society increased.
And so I began, just on my own, introducing ways to help my students stay in the room
when discomfort was presented to them, to show them that learning has to have an element
of discomfort and that when this agreement is done well, it's a wonderful opportunity for
connection for learning, for growth, for innovation. And like Dan and I often say, for
human connection. Disagreement should be the beginning of the conversation, not the
end. And so I haven't invented anything in this field. I use a lot of methodologies that
have been modelled and experimented on by other academics, and I've just started
implementing it in my classroom.
And then I was lucky enough to cross paths with Dan, when he was doing his graduate
studies in psychology. He actually did it in the Graduate Diploma, which I used to direct,
and now I'm Assistant Director. So once he graduated, he reached out to me and mentioned
that he had this idea of a project and whether I was interested in collaborating with him,
and I certainly was. It was an opportunity to go beyond my classroom and my school and
make this work more meaningful across our whole university. And then from then, we can
probably talk about it over the coming hour, but obviously Brave Conversations has now
become a national - Monash-led but a national program, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: We certainly will come to that in a moment. Was the birth of the
initiative related to what you saw playing out in campus in the months after October 2023?
Was that a particular impetus?
DR ZAID: That began earlier, but I'm actually going to pass it to Dan, because I know the
impetus for Dan was - maybe not what was happening on campus but certainly October 7
had a really personal impact on him, and I'd like to invite Dan to speak to that a little bit.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, of course.

DR HELLER: Thanks, Farid. As a historian, I'm always fascinated by when we mark
a turning point, and there is sometimes a danger in treating the events of October 7 and the
Gaza war that followed as the place where we begin this story, because one thing I think
Farid and I do agree on is that polarisation and the - its impact on our society has been
something that has been there long before October 7 and that so many of the dynamics that
we saw in how hatred and prejudice played out in the months that followed, there were
ingredients already there.
So, for me, I had thought after graduating - well, not after but as I was working in this
degree for psychology, that I was just going to leave these tools in my classroom. It was
going to be an island sort of refuge where young people who wanted to escape the
polarisation that is especially exacerbated in social media, who wanted a space where they
can say "I don't know", "I'm uncertain", I just thought that's what the classroom was going
to be. And then on October 7, two colleagues, two people that I know who are Jewish,
were killed when Hamas invaded the south of Israel, and then about 10 to 11 days later
a colleague of mine's father-in-law, his family, about 75 people were killed when a missile
struck their apartment building in Khan Yunis.
So in the field that I'm in, teaching Palestinian and Israeli history, I've had a great privilege
and I know it makes me very odd to have friends across divides, and what that means is
that in those early weeks and in all the weeks that followed, there's just been a lot of
heartbreak from people that I know and care deeply about. So in the wake of that
happening in those early weeks of October 7 - I don't really know how to say this in
a sanitised way. My heart kind of broke open, and I felt this sense of crisis.
I knew that the work I was doing as a historian in the classroom mattered, but I also felt
this deep urgency to try and bring some of those skills and to see if there was anyone else
at the university who wanted to be able to help support our community in a really, really
difficult moment and to make sure that we didn't cut off communication and that we didn't
believe that every disagreement was one to be terrified of. So that's where Brave
Conversations Project began for me.
I once heard someone say - and this is someone who lost a child in this conflict before
October 7 - that grief is nuclear and that it has the capacity to be an energy that can create
so much destruction and so much hatred and so much violence, but grief can, also as
a nuclear force, be used to cultivate compassion, to bring good in the world, to honour
people's memory. And this project for me, I know for many of the students that come to
us, is a way of coping with this moment and a way of trying to honour the memory of
people who don't have the luxury and the privilege of living in this great country and to be
living with an opportunity for peace. And it is also a form of protest, I suppose, at the
polarisation that really does threaten us all.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your description of the Brave Conversations Project uses the
expression "constructive disagreement" often. Could you explain what you saw in the
classroom in terms of the way students were interacting that led you to think that this
process of constructive disagreement had to be taught?

DR ZAID: I can. And I know I speak for Dan here as well. He might jump in with
a couple of extra thoughts. But we both saw conversations in the classroom play out along
really rigid lines and the response was either one of two things, both of which we found
deeply problematic - we still find deeply problematic. One is self-censorship and violence
and the majority of students adopt that perspective, "I would rather not say anything
because I don't know what's acceptable and what's not", and, more importantly, "I don't
want to hurt or upset anyone and because I don't know what language to use, I'm going to
self-censor and not share my perspective". So the majority of my students and Dan's
students adopted that viewpoint. In fact, the majority of academics and colleagues that we
work with often adopt that viewpoint. When things get tense and there’s disagreement,
self-censorship is the safest option.
The other way that students and our colleagues sometimes respond is to perform certainty.
We know what is virtuous, what is moral and what is right, and anyone who disagrees is,
in one way or another, morally reprehensible. And for us, that's problematic as well,
because as academics, as human beings, and engaged citizens, we want to model humility
and admitting when we are not sure, but still having the courage to ask unfinished
questions, to stumble our way towards a better understanding together.
And so constructive disagreement is trying to encourage that middle perspective of you
don't need to pretend that you know all the answers, and you don't need to sit there in
silence. Let's come together. Dan has this beautiful metaphor. We set the table. We
encourage people to bring their most authentic and sincere selves, whether they're
half-formed, half-finished, probably misguided perspectives, and together, through seeing
each other's humanity and dignity, we can come to a better understanding, but not
performing or pretending that we already have the answer before the conversation even
began.
So constructive disagreement is just a framework. There's many ways of calling it. We
have colleagues that joke, it has to start with a C and it has to start with a D. It could be
civil dialogue. There's about half a dozen of CD terms that all point to the same direction.
And it's just a way or a framework where we can come together with humility, with
compassion, with open-mindedness and just try and figure it out, without the risk of
punishment or counselling, for lack of a better term. So hopefully that sums up for you
what we're trying to allude to when we say constructive disagreement. It is a way of
leaning into disagreement and trying to gain a better understanding of each other's
humanity and under story. Anything to add?
DR HELLER: I might only add that this might land - this might surprise anyone that's
hearing this. We thought, when we started doing this work, that it would require some
deeply intricate choreography and that it would be like pulling teeth, and the opposite is
true. When you tell people and you are creating the conditions for authentic human
connection, when you say to people, "We are inviting you to be the best versions of
yourself: calm, kind, curious, compassionate", more often than not, people rise to the
occasion. And I think the reason why that surprises us - and, again, it goes back to
humility - is, like so many others, we presume that what we see on social media or we see

on the news in terms of human behaviour is an accurate reflection of humanity, of the
people that we live with in the community.
DR ZAID: Of society.
DR HELLER: That's right. And it has been such an extraordinarily hopeful experience
every time we run a session, every time we work with our students, to see that that's not the
case.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask about the sessions, because you've indicated that Brave
Conversations Project offers generally three different types of workshops which are
targeted to, first, educators of any level, experience and faculty; second, university
leadership team; and, thirdly, student leaders. Why have you identified those specific
groups as the participants or the targets of your workshop program?
DR HELLER: So just as a quick aside, we have run workshops for other groups as well.
We have run workshops outside of the universities, but just to focus on the university
itself, one of the core foundations that we're working with is this idea of an ecological
approach, that when we are working with a community as complex and diverse as
a university, we need to try and engage all levels of the community, and that different
sectors in the university community will have different needs, different levels of expertise
or experience.
I think that despite that, all of the workshops that we run do have common threads. The
first is we talk about the different values that people can bring into difficult conversations,
things like humanity, curiosity, courage. We talk about the skillsets that people can bring
in, and mindsets as well. I will share just one example of a mindset, and this comes from
colleagues in the United States. Often times when we engage in disagreement around
polarising issues, we adopt a warrior mindset and we - whether subconsciously or not, our
aim is to win the conversation.
So when we're listening to someone - if Farid and I were having a disagreement and I'm
listening to Farid with the aim to defeat him, my attention is going to narrow so - in such
a narrow fashion that I might be missing out on really key information. We invite people
instead to adopt an explorer's mindset. So before you set out to try and challenge
someone's views, why not first pause, take a beat and ask the question how did we even
come to see the same thing in such fundamentally different ways? Why don't we explore
the values, the life experiences that led this other person to the journey of their position and
maybe also, in doing so, reflect a little bit about our own life and our experience. It
connects back to this point about humility. None of us in the world can fully
comprehensively and accurately perceive the entire world around us in all of its
complexity.
DR ZAID: Yes. Just to add, when we work to supplement, the ecological approach just
means we are trying to engage as many stakeholders and build as many relationships as
possible. So in a university setting, obviously, it's the leadership team, it's academics and
the students. That covers all of it. But not quite. There's also thousands, at Monash, of

professional staff who support the running of the university and, of course, we reach out
and now have engaged with them into a multi-term, multi-semester programs to support
them to be able to have Brave Conversations and to build a better workplace culture.
When we work with high schools, of course, we deal with the students, with the teachers,
the principals, but we also engage the parents because for children engaged in this space,
the parents have to be a large part of the engagement. Without them, very little benefit or
advancement can occur. And so the ecological approach just means trying to ascertain
who is - what kind of stakeholders are in the space that we're operating and how can we
best build relationships with all of them and help them build relationships with one
another.
DR HELLER: If I may just add one other thing - and thank you for your patience.
Another core part of what we do is to say there are no quick fixes. That if we enter into
any difficult conversation to try to solve it as quickly as possible, we are setting ourselves
up for failure. So many of the issues that are plaguing Australian society involve tensions
that are irreconcilable. They're never going to go away. So we try to shift the aim to be
thinking about how we navigate tensions wisely together, instead of trying once and -
DR ZAID: Through time.
DR HELLER: That's right. Through time and through relationship rather than simply
saying, you know, pick a side, choose X or choose Y and that's it.
DR ZAID: Become comfortable with a lack of closure, we often say. There often is no
closure with the conversations - the difficult conversations we have. And that's part of the
process. If everyone can accept at the beginning that we are not going to get to closure, the
conversation unfolds in a much more holistic way, because no one is trying to win and
prove the other person wrong or the other group wrong.
MR LANCASTER SC: And, indeed, you have referred in your statement to conditions in
the classroom that punish nuance, in your expression, and that your workshops are
designed to address that problem. What happens, in your experience, when educators are
unwilling or afraid to address contested issues in an educational setting, in a classroom or
a lecture?
DR HELLER: So we are very, very, very privileged to work with extraordinary
educators not just at Monash but now across multiple universities in Australia. The stakes
are high for many of them, especially if they are sessional instructors that are working
from, you know, semester to semester and they don't have the benefit of knowing that their
job is going to be secure. The typical response is to avoid a topic altogether. So it is very
easy as an instructor, when you are working in a context where the stakes are very high,
where if, heaven forbid, something is misinterpreted, the public trial that can happen over
social media is actually itself the punishment.
DR ZAID: Or the official complaint.

DR HELLER: Or an official complaint.
DR ZAID: Or the end of semester review of your teaching practices.
DR HELLER: That's right. It is just that fear, I think, overpowers many educators, and I
think that that in part explains why they avoid difficult topics. What we try to remind
educators of is that in the absence of being able to talk about this in the university, our
students are going to be looking for information elsewhere. So in that silence of the
majority of people that aren't extreme, extremists on social media, they fill the gap, the
conflict entrepreneurs that are deliberately looking to inflame emotions, to radicalise in
whichever way you imagine. They are the ones that our students are turning to.
So we really do have a mission to do this. We also, in terms of the leadership at
universities, have a mission to make sure they are protecting their educators and supporting
them with training and also letting them know that in the event that there are complaints
that come up, that the university is there to support them through that process as well, not
just the students.
DR ZAID: And I think maybe, if I may, this is a good opportunity to just also quickly
discuss this concept of care and harm. I care about my students deeply. So does Dan. In
fact, I have never met another fellow colleague or academic across Australia that at least
admits explicitly that they do not care about their students. Educators and teachers at
every level get into this profession because they deeply care about students and they want
to avoid harming them. I do. Dan does. Everyone does. But how that plays out differs,
and, in fact, Dan and I disagree with a lot of our colleagues who think - and I don't mean
just at Monash; this is a broad philosophy - to care for students and to avoid harm means to
avoid any discussion of contentious issues, just by coddling and completely sanitising the
class from any contention, they provide the best care.
And I'll speak for myself - I know Dan agrees as well - we disagree. We don't think that
avoidance equates to care. In fact, we feel as educators we have a responsibility to expose
our students to ideas that challenge their world view, that challenge the way that they
conceive the world works. Because if we don't, if we don't provide the environment and
the safe space in the classroom to be wrong, to make mistakes, to ask that half-finished
question - because are you asking from a place of ignorance and you want to find out
more. If we don't allow our students that space to make mistakes and to trip without
repercussion, then they'll just leave - after a couple of years, they will leave our
classrooms, they will leave our universities and then they are in society, and they will
absolutely be exposed to horrendous ideas every single day.
And if they haven't had a chance to practise having to navigate these tensions and haven't
been introduced to the skills and the tools needed to better be able to deal with difficult
conversations and difficult relationships, then I would feel that I've done my students
a disservice and, honestly, that's the fundamental reason that drives my passion for this
work, for Brave Conversations.

MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. Can I ask some practical questions about the
workshops program. It's right you have delivered workshops to more than 1200 Monash
educators? Does that sound about right?
DR HELLER: Correct.
DR ZAID: Yes. About 12 or 13 hundred Monash educators and close to six or seven
hundred nationally now. So we are coming to up 2000 educators on every level, and that's
just university educators.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you mentioned from time to time you deliver workshops
outside of the education system? Is that right?
DR ZAID: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can you describe that briefly?
DR HELLER: Yes. Sure. I'll admit, this surprised the heck out of us. When we started
doing this work, we started getting requests from different sectors in civil society that we
never would have thought would have any interest. So we have been very, very lucky to
be able to work with high schools. We're in our second year of piloting a program with the
young people. We - I'm trying to think -
DR ZAID: With galleries, with museums, with local councils with, multiple departments
of federal and state government. The truth is - and like Dan said - this initially surprised
us. It no longer does, because we understand why. But when people hear Brave
Conversations and that there's a workshop to be able to bring people to encourage them to
ask authentic and sincere questions and to build relationships, almost everybody instantly
thinks, okay, that will benefit my workplace or this culture that I'm a part of or this group.
And so we have just been invited and we've been very grateful to have engaged with
various sectors and various levels of government. Everybody sees a need for this type of
work. And - were you going to say something else?
DR HELLER: No, no, no.
DR ZAID: Yes. We're trying to balance. After all is said and done, Dan and I are
lifetime educators. We are academics. We're passionate and grateful to have the jobs we
do. We selected it and have been grateful and lucky to have been given this opportunity.
So our number one priority is the education sector, both university and high school. But
we are just sharing that there's a lot of desire and need for this type of work well beyond
the education sector.
MR LANCASTER SC: And how are they delivered or how are they undertaken? Is it
face-to-face in a small group setting? Is that the standard?

DR HELLER: A wonderful question. So I think that one of the tensions - speaking of
tensions - that any government will wrestle with when trying to combat polarisation is the
tension between doing things at scale, you know, a kind of massive program, and making
sure that learning and genuine human connection is actually happening. There have been
studies - of the studies, of the mega studies - looking at different types of interventions to
reduce bias that are online modules where they're -
DR ZAID: One time.
DR HELLER: One time, one shot, you know, and the results are not particularly
promising. Typically, no significant change of people's points of view, and if there is
a little bit of a change, it tends to drop off after two weeks. So, for us, the key is
relationship and the opportunity to do this over time. And this too, there is some research
to suggest as well that these are the best types of interventions, the ones that actually
involved face-to-face interactions with people's whose views are different than our own.
Some of this is built on research that shows that human beings are spectacularly awful at
imagining someone else's life experience. So we often say imagine if you were in their
shoes. Actually, most of us can't do that. So, once again, that explains the benefit of being
with someone and having the capacity to ask curious questions and to learn as you go.
DR ZAID: Speaking of scale, yes, Dan and I were the original directors of Brave
Conversations, but Monash has invested heavily into this program. And so late last year,
we actually ran a three-day long workshop for 30 academics from every single faculty at
Monash University. And the program is called Brave Conversation Ambassadors. And
the reason we did that is because we wanted to officially make this embedded in our
university culture, and we wanted to have representatives - well, the university wanted to
have representatives for every single faculty, so that these ambassadors can then take the
concepts and themes of Brave Conversations back into their fields of expertise and engage
with their fellow colleagues on a level that possibly Dan and I couldn't engage with
because we don't have that shared lived experience of what it's like to teach podiatry or law
or a hundred other topics. And so that was really, really important. There's only so much
that Dan and I can do. We love what we do. But making this scalable to some regard and
sustainable has meant that we've actually expanded well beyond just the two of us.
MR LANCASTER SC: Was the same idea behind the - I understand there is a national
student leadership retreat. Was that undertaken for a similar purpose?
DR ZAID: Yep.
DR HELLER: The idea was to bring together people who otherwise would have never
had the opportunity to meet, from different corners of Australia, different life experiences,
different world views, and it wasn't simply to teach them the skills of constructive dialogue
and disagreement. It was to empower them with tools that they could bring back to their
student organisations to be able to integrate these into the work that they do. If anybody
wants to experience deep hope, take a group of university students out for a couple of days
and, look, I wish I could tell you that it was a function of the deep workshops that we did.

My hunch is that 70 per cent of the meaningful connections across difference that
happened had nothing to do with us. It was in those quiet moments where -
DR ZAID: We weren't there.
DR HELLER: We weren't there. You just give people permission to, again, be their best
selves, ask curious questions, stay in the room when things feel a bit of discomfort, and the
most extraordinary things can happen.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your work has been endorsed by the Group of Eight's Expert
Advisory Committee on Combatting Antisemitism, and you have observed in your
submission that while Brave Conversations Project is not a project about antisemitism, it is
a project that you think reduces antisemitism. Could you elaborate on that?
DR HELLER: Sure. So our work is not meant to be replacement for work around
protecting the Jewish community, security, work around some very serious political
questions which our country is wrestling with. Our work is thinking about the bottom-up
and making sure that we are engaging communities and engaging Australians at an
individual level to be able to build capacity and commitment, to protecting the democratic
virtues that, if done well and if adopted, can support the diverse and very special society
we have here.
The reason why we made a choice to focus on a skillset for polarising issues rather than
focus on one issue is in part because we believe deeply that, firstly, so many of the issues
that have exacerbated antisemitism are a function of broader social forces that have been
unfolding in Australian society and elsewhere globally, whether it's the advent of social
media, whether it's the impact of the COVID on young people. There's just a million and
one different things that aren't unique to the challenges that have arisen about antisemitism.
But the other reason why I think our work can be useful is that - again, this concept will
sound slightly cynical, but it does come, again, from lots of research on anti-bias
training - our deepest fear is when you bring educators, you bring anyone into a program
that is only with one specific issue and it's within a workplace context, the question that

Zakat. I wanted to ask you about that and how that concept at the time resonated for you

RABBI KASTEL AM: Yes, as the Commissioner would be aware from my brother
Mendel's statement, the word "mitzvah" is really important in Jewish tradition. And so for
me - and I think my mother modelled that way of being, that life was about obeying
mitzvahs, doing what is right and contributing. And it was fascinating for me to see these
young people really motivated by their own version of the idea of a mitzvah. And at the
time, the theme of our work was goodness and kindness, and the children were very
enthusiastic from a spiritual, Islamic motivation base to contribute to do good in the world,
and that moved me greatly.
MS PHILLIPS: Is it right that Together for Humanity was formally founded a couple of
years after that visit that you have just been referring to, and it was founded with the aim of
fostering understanding between people from diverse backgrounds and encouraging
positive and respectful relationships between them?
RABBI KASTEL AM: That's correct. And over time also, it had a greater emphasis on
belonging as another expression of that same aim.

MS PHILLIPS: And you have now worked as an intercultural educator for around 25
years; is that right?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And today, the Together for Humanity Foundation is a not-for-profit
educational organisation that works with schools, predominantly, to reduce prejudice and,
as you just said, foster a sense of belonging amongst young people?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you tell me at a high level how the organisation goes about
achieving that aim in terms of its engagement and programming both with schools and
their teachers.
RABBI KASTEL AM: Yes. So at a high level, there are five main activities. One is
working with young people directly, face-to-face, giving them opportunities to engage with
people that they might never meet otherwise, people with a migration story, like Dr Beau
here. Also, as the previous evidence you heard this morning, modelling co-existence and
goodwill between people from different backgrounds and enabling young people to
flourish and to question, to - we empower young people to participate in discussion and
drive their own learning.
That's one part. The other part is working with teachers and enabling them, supporting
their efforts so they feel both confident and competent to do what they need to do in order
for students to be inclusive and to have intercultural understanding. In addition to
face-to-face, we also do that online. We engage communities, parents and families of
young people. And another part that Dr Beau can speak to is partnerships, which is
actually helping schools identify an opportunity or a challenge and to transform the school
so that it's sustainable and they own it and drive that change.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Rabbi, you have noted in your witness statement that the programs
that Together for Humanity delivers are not focused on any one type of prejudice but they
concentrate on addressing all prejudices. Can I ask why is that, for you, an important
feature of the organisation's work?
RABBI KASTEL AM: It's important because there are two things that are true. One is
that specific kinds of prejudice do need to be addressed. It's not good enough to tell young
people, "Say no to racism" because it doesn't work enough of the time. People make
excuses. "I'm not racist but". You see that with Islamophobia figures and, of course, with
antisemitism. So people - and there was a lot of anti-Chinese sentiment during COVID.
So telling people a general message of don't be racist doesn't cut it. We do need to address
specific kinds of prejudices and for young people to understand the differences between
those prejudices, and to learn to reject all of those prejudices.
At the same time, in our experience, our success is very much driven by the fact that we
are impartial - politically impartial and we are inclusive and care about all communities,

and that resonates and moves young people very strongly when they can see, for example,
a Muslim woman talking passionately about antisemitism or a Jewish rabbi talking about
Islamophobia, or First Nations people talking about other people's prejudices and being
supported by people from different backgrounds. So rather than people pleading for
themselves, it's a plea for reasonableness. It's a plea for all of us thriving.
MS PHILLIPS: And in the delivery of that kind of work and programming, are you able
to comment on the role played by the Together for Humanity educators and where they're
drawn from and some of their backgrounds?
RABBI KASTEL AM: I'll give you an example. The late Peter Lazar was one of the
leaders of PR in Australia. But he also had a unique story as a migrant. He grew up in
Vienna and had a glimpse of Hitler as a young child. He came to talk to a group of
students, alongside a Muslim presenter and a Coptic Orthodox man, a Greek Egyptian.
And the Coptic Orthodox man said, beautifully, "This is my brother and this is my sister"
and spoke effusively to the young people and modelled that idea of co-existence, and then
invited the children to think about what they heard and to be curious.
And one child said to the Greek Orthodox man aren't you - sorry, the Greek Coptic
Christian and he said, "Aren't you a traitor to your people considering what has been
happening in Egypt? Aren't you a traitor to your people by calling Muslims and Jews your
brothers and sisters?" And it was that question that led to a very rich discussion for young
people to think about loyalties and connections between people and the ways in which we
navigate loyalties. So that's one part of the work, is that modelling.
Another part of the role of the presenters is, as Peter did, to share personal stories. We
know that empathy is a big driver against prejudice. And when you can imagine this
grown man being a little child and seeing this historical figure in the way that he changed
the world and you put yourself in that person's shoes for a moment, it broadens your
horizons. So storytelling is a very, very important of the role of the people going to
schools.
And another part is really inviting young people to make their own sense. I've had
permission to bring a prop, which I will do now. One of the things that I talk to young
people about and we talk to young people about is the way that, when they are young, we
ask them to reflect on maybe a little brother or sister and the way that they're wide open,
full of wonder, learning about the world, making new friends and then something happens.
Because as their bodies grow, their spirits begin to shrink, and often by the time they get to
year 7 and high school, they've snapped shut.
And we ask young people to think about the impact that they have on each other's
experience of wellbeing. What does it feel like? How do you affect other people's ability
to be themselves, to be open, to participate, to make new friends or to be guarded? And
young people will tell us it's the judgments, the expectations, the drip-feed of
comments - of racist comments, nasty comments, judgments. And we invite them to think
about those.

If I can just give another brief example. One school we worked with had a culture of
pretending that these jokes were all funny. And we asked them to step forward if they
were ever in a situation where they knew in their heart that something that was said was
wrong but they felt pressure to pretend it was okay, to pretend it was funny. And a vast
number of students stepped forward. And in that moment, the students had an opportunity
to think about what kind of norms they want for their school. What kind of norms - what
do they want the peer pressure to be about? And by stepping forward they can see they
were not alone in their sense that something was wrong in the culture of that school at that
particular time.
MS PHILLIPS: Thank you, Rabbi. You have mentioned the diversity that exists within
the education teams that come in and give presentations with Together for Humanity. Are
you able to comment on whether that diversity sees reflection at the leadership level within
the organisation?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Absolutely. We - one of the qualities of Together for Humanity
is that authenticity, the spirit, as it were. And it became clear to us that if we are to talk
about co-existence and we are to talk about coming Together for Humanity, hence the
name, we have got to be that in our own practice. And so we established a tradition within
the organisation to have a board of people from diverse backgrounds. Our president is
a Muslim educator. Our chairman, who is another leadership role, is a Buddhist. We have
got Jewish people on the Board. Various other backgrounds and, of course, different kinds
of expertise in media, education, law and so on. But the cultural and religious diversity of
our board is one of the principles that ensures our integrity and our authenticity in terms of
the message we say to young people.
MS PHILLIPS: Rabbi, before I come to Dr Hu-Jia, I'd like to ask you this. You have
said in your statement that Together for Humanity's programs focus on building the
capabilities that underpin social cohesion. Are you able to outline at a high level what you
see those capabilities as including?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Absolutely. In the first instance, it's the ability to empathise with
out-groups. So what we know from social science is that empathy is essentially geared to
the clan, to us, and, therefore, while research tells us that empathy is key to defeating kinds
prejudices, if empathy is just geared to us, it's a problem. And so inviting young people to
think about us and them, to think about who is Australian and who is not Australian, so
that capacity to have reflective empathy with people who might be seen as an "other" is an
important capability. It's part of also broader intercultural understanding, which has, as
part of that, is also reflecting on your own identity, knowing yourself so that then you can
know others. Respectful dialogue, curiosity, those are some of the high-level capabilities
that we are focused on.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Hu-Jia, you have said that you are the National School Partnerships
Manager at Together for Humanity Foundation?
DR HU-JIA: Yes, that's correct.

MS PHILLIPS: You have been in that role since August of 2023?
DR HU-JIA: Yes, almost three years.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you explain your main responsibilities within that role?
DR HU-JIA: Certainly. My main responsibility is overseeing our National School
Partnerships Program. I work with schools across Australia to work with them to develop
and strengthen their intercultural understanding, particularly to come up with projects that
strengthen students' and teachers' professional learning around intercultural understanding,
inclusion and belonging and to address issues of different types of prejudice.
MS PHILLIPS: I'll come back a little bit later to ask you about some of the finer details
of the school partnerships program that you mentioned. Can I ask some questions about
your own background. Is it right that before coming to Together for Humanity, you
worked as the Education Programs Director at the Asia Education Foundation through the
University of Melbourne?
DR HU-JIA: I was one of the Education Coordinators at Asia Education Foundation,
a part of a group called Asia Link at the University of Melbourne. My work at Asia
Education Foundation was around global citizenship education, Asian literacy and
intercultural understanding.
MS PHILLIPS: And prior to having that role, you had more than 10 years of experience
teaching in school and university settings in Australia and also in the United Kingdom?
DR HU-JIA: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And are you able to tell us about your various academic qualifications
which you have listed at paragraph 6 of your statement?
DR HU-JIA: Yes. So I have a Bachelor of Arts in English from Jiangxi Agricultural
University in China, and also I have a Masters of Teaching Chinese as a Foreign Language
from the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom. Also I have a Masters of Arts in

China, and also I hold a PhD in Education from the University of Melbourne.
MS PHILLIPS: Are you able to outline what your doctoral research focused on?
DR HU-JIA: Yes, so my doctoral research focused on Australian-born Chinese children's
multilingual experiences and their identity formation process.
MS PHILLIPS: You have said in your statement - this is at paragraph 7 - that
a consistent focus throughout your academic and professional life has been understanding
how young people form perceptions of identity and difference, develop a sense of
belonging and engage constructively around cultural and other diversity; is that right?

DR HU-JIA: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: You have also said in your statement that your interest in intercultural
understanding is informed not only by your academic and professional experience, but also
by your own lived experience. Are you able to explain that?
DR HU-JIA: Yes, I can. So as I said in my statement, I was born and grew up in China
and migrated to Australia. So questions of identity and belonging, they are not just
academic terms. They are actually concepts that are very relevant to my own experience.
So at Together for Humanity from time to time, I co-facilitate a program called Migration
Stories to students, alongside with my colleagues from other diverse backgrounds in
Victoria. So a common example that appeared in that workshop with students is that
question around "Where are you from?"
So students of diverse cultural backgrounds in modern Australian classrooms, they tell us
they are comfortable with that question, but not with a repeated follow-up, "Where are you
really from?" So during our conversation with students in these workshops, we work with
the students. We have a conversation around identity and belonging, and we highlight and
also unpack the complexity of those terms, such as identity and belonging. They are
highly contextual. Some Australian-born students or children with migrant family, they
might highly identify as Australian, whereas some students, they are more close to the
country of their origin or the cultural heritage of their parents' place of origin, and
sometimes they are both.
So - and even for one person and in different contexts, different scenarios, depending on
who they are communicating with, one part of their identity may be more prominent than
the other. So those concepts are very dynamic. So, however, if we look at media
discussions in the public discourse around the identity of being Australian and of being
a migrant, those statuses are very fixed. And so during these conversations with students
in our workshop, we really encourage them to think out of the box, to view those concepts
as a dynamic situation or constructs.
MS PHILLIPS: At paragraph 9 of your statement, Dr Hu-Jia, you've provided an
example of some research interviews that you participated in concerning young people's
experiences of identity and belonging. Would you care to share that example with us?
DR HU-JIA: Yes. So this is related to my previous research project. So in my fieldwork
and in a classroom in Melbourne - it's a primary school - a student, she is the only non-
Anglo-Australian student in the classroom and from one of the countries in Asia Pacific.
So every time in the classroom when questions arose around that country or culture or
political challenges and this student was positioned and in practice as the representative of
that country and culture and people and the government. So the student was very stressed
and she felt she had to carry this burden, and, yes, so that's the example.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've stated in your witness statement that, from your perspective,
that example illustrates how young people from minority backgrounds can sometimes

experience pressure to act as representatives of broader cultural, national or ethnic groups,
which can affect their sense of belonging and inclusion within the school environment.
DR HU-JIA: Exactly. And I do believe Australian children in our classrooms should not
be held to account for government of another country or the culture of another country,
yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Hu-Jia, at paragraph 11 of your statement you refer to how your
personal context has reinforced your commitment to supporting initiatives that promote
inclusion, that challenge prejudice and that strengthen social cohesion among young
people. And you have said when you're asked about your work, you say it's not only
something that you do but something that you are living day-to-day. Can you explain that
concept, please.
DR HU-JIA: Yes, that's correct. So during our workshop with students, we encourage
open conversation. We create a safe space where students can ask any questions, as long
as it's from a place of curiosity instead of a judgment. So often some students would ask
me why you do the work you do. And at Together for Humanity, the key concept is
around belonging. So the vision of Together for Humanity is an Australia where all
students feel they belong. And so the concept of "belonging" is not just, you know,
a terminology; it's me, myself, as a Chinese Australian, as a migrant to this country, and
I do want to feel I belong and I do want to share my experience of prejudice or
discrimination in different circumstances with students, and to model that we are able to,
we should have those courageous conversations and hoping that one of the students, you
know, in auditorium can relate to my experience and would have the courage to speak up
and also for their peers to stand up when they see something is not right in the school
community. Yes. So by sharing my own story I want to feel like I can contribute to this
country in terms of social cohesion from a personal level, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: I'd like to ask you some more details about the Together for Humanity
School Partnership Program that you are a coordinator of, and you've addressed that from
paragraph 15 of your witness statement. You've identified that the program supports
schools to embed intercultural understanding across policies, practices, and teaching and
learning initiatives. Are you able to step us through how the program is rolled out into
schools by Together for Humanity in practice?
DR HU-JIA: Yes, certainly. So the formal name of that program is called Intercultural
Understanding Partnership Program. So I will refer to it as a school partnership, program,
for clarity. So it's funded by the Commonwealth Department of Education and so provides
eligible schools up to $10,000 in support and Together for Humanity's educational
services, and to address intercultural learning priority or challenge in the school
community.
So it's open to schools across all sectors, government, Catholic and independent. So the
process is once a school identifies intercultural priority or challenge in the school such as
racism, or they apply - they put in an application with a proposed project and, if selected,

we work with the school to design, with a culturally responsive action plan to address that
challenge or intercultural priority.
So a very important principle is that schools are leading the project, because school context
is very complex and each school has their own unique challenge or need. So we respect
that and we do believe schools understand their circumstances the best. So whereas
Together for Humanity we provide funding, educational programs as requested, or any
other support we're able to provide.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've referred to one use of the funds that schools can receive
under that program as being enabling schools to fund relief teachers to carry out regular
classroom work. Can you explain why that can be a helpful source of funding in this
space?
DR HU-JIA: Yes. So the funding can be used for a few different areas, including staff or
teacher release. And we note schools are very busy places, and even for very committed
teachers or staff and their capacity is limited, we don't want this partnership to be add on,
to be a burden to the school. So that means for a very dedicated teacher they have to teach
and have to supervise students and also have to carry out this project.
So that's why part of the grant can go direct, can direct to staff release or teacher release.
So the teacher or the principal or the coordinator, the program coordinator at the school,
can focus on the project without, you know, consuming too much of their capacity.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Hu-Jia, at paragraph 19 of your statement, you've noted that
wherever possible the program, when it's introduced in schools, seeks to adopt
a whole-of-school approach. Can you explain what that involves, a-whole-of-school
approach?
DR HU-JIA: Yes. So a whole-of-school approach is based on the rationale that one
single social challenge or intercultural learning priority is not for one reason. So it's
multiple factors will contribute to a challenge such as racism; and so that's why we need
multiple players that will take actions in a school community to address that issue. So the
whole-of-school approach we start it with the school leader, a school leadership team.
So once the school has been successful in securing that grant and also establish their
partner with us, so the school needs to have a dedicated school-based partnership team,
that consists of school leadership, school principal, teachers or other key staff members, as
well as student representatives and community representatives, depending on the project,
such as Elders from the local Aboriginal communities to be on that - to be in that planning
phase.
So from the planning, they adopt the whole-of-school approach. All the key players, they
contribute to the planning of that project. And in the implementation phase which means
all the actors, they have to share some of the responsibilities of that project. So we don't
really rely on one person. Yes. So that is what we mean by whole-of-school approach.

MS PHILLIPS: You have expanded in your statement, perhaps, on that concept by
noting that the overall aim of the program isn't to fund individual activities within
individual schools but to support schools to develop sustainable and tailored approaches to
strengthening belonging and inclusion or, where necessary, to respond to prejudice and
prevent it.
DR HU-JIA: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you explain how that kind of sustainable approach is able to be
realised within school settings in practice?
DR HU-JIA: Yes. Absolutely. In this intercultural learning space we've seen so many
activities. They are one of the activities. For example, during Harmony Week a school
might invite a cultural group to do dancing, you know, in the school, and that's it. So that
cultural exposure is important, it's very critical, but we want to go beyond that, and design
interventions that can last.
For example, if part of the grant can be directed to curriculum development or policy
revision in the school setting, and that change can be more sustained. So even after the
funded period or after the single activity and there is a legacy there, and so if it's already
embedded in the curriculum it can be more sustainable.
For example, in 2025 we supported a school in South Australia and part of - a significant
proportion of that funding directed to release teachers, so they could have the time to write
a new curriculum, a unit of work regarding global citizenship education, yes, which is
a very important part in the intercultural learning space. So because it's in the curriculum,
and so we are very content that the project can be carried out even after the funding period,
yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Thank you. Rabbi Kastel, can I return to you and ask you about some
particular examples of Together for Humanity's work that you've touched on in your
witness statement. At paragraph 16 of your statement, you have described a professional
development session that was conducted in July this year for primary school teachers and
how this modelled the way that trust can be built. Can you share your experience of that
session with us?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Yes. So in July of 2026, I found myself kind of returning to the
very beginning of my journey and feeling - I met with the school prior to the professional
session, learning session with teachers in May 2026. I, for the first time, again, was
hesitant to be seen looking Jewish. At this time, instead of a white disguise, I had
a ridiculous kind of straw hat. And when I reflected on that, I thought "No, no, I don't
need to go back there" and I told the teachers "When I came to the school that last time in
May when I came here, I had the straw hat, but today I'm wearing my yarmulke and
I choose to be who I am in this space."
And I was - there were three of us on the day. There was a Muslim woman in a hijab;
there was an Anglo-Celtic looking, sort of, man. When we first started the conversation it

was a little bit heavy, the context of what we were talking about; and the fact that the
Royal Commission is happening was also a background to the conversation in a sense that
perhaps a rabbi walking into a school where a lot of the teachers were of Muslim
background, maybe this was about one community, about antisemitism exclusively.
I, again, used the expandable ball and talked about "This is what we're about, we're about
your students and about the teachers as well" because teachers, as was referred to earlier
this morning, often feel fear and anxious about what they can do at school. So some
teachers sometimes become quite closed as well as the children. And I invited them,
I said, "What we want to do in this session is to actually open up." And they did. I mean,
they were incredibly generous and welcoming.
It was tense until one of the teachers complimented me on my socks. They were fairly
conservative socks; they were not particularly interesting. But it just broke the ice where
we connected as people. And teachers talked about their experiences of the questions they
ask, the social media that the children are exposed to, and how do they help young people
navigate that and were encouraged to recognise that they knew a lot of the answers to their
own questions and to really support them and saying "In your question is an implicit
answer. You've got this."
I think it's often more a confidence problem than a competence problem. And I'm pleased
to say that by the end of the session there was definitely a feeling of openness, of easy - of
laughter, of connection.
MS PHILLIPS: And can I take you, please, to paragraph 23 of your statement. You've
referred there to some sessions that were conducted for some Year 7 students in a school in
around the middle of 2025 that explored Aboriginal history and, in particular,
a significance of a Welcome to Country. And you go on to refer to the impact that some of
that work had on the school community. Are you able to expand on that for us?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Certainly. So this is - I did refer to this case study previously.
This was a school where there were some significant problems of antisemitism. There
were anti-Asian, particularly anti-Chinese, comments that were made. And as I said
earlier, there was a culture of pretending this was okay. I mean, there were some horrific
antisemitic things that were said at that school that were very distressing to some students
at the school. And the school initially reached out to us just to talk with the students. We
spent six days with the students.
We had youth leaders from the Jewish community by BJE, who I know came and
presented at this Commission. When we first came in October '24, there was a sense
that - there was an unease in the school culture. The school then, after an initial experience
with us, with small groups - so it was multiple sessions, but it was a once-off intervention
or twice-off intervention, large group and small group sessions - were encouraged to apply
for a partnership that was administered by Dr Hu-Jia.
And that actually really was a game changer for the school because part of that was us
working with the teachers, but what it led to, as was described - as he described so well

previously is the school taking ownership of this. And so the teachers then began to train
student leaders, older student leaders, to become their in-house trainers. And so in May
'25, it wasn't us doing the work; it was the school doing the work.
So older students developed their own training for younger students with talking about
Welcome to Country, a connect game to find connections between people of different
cultures. They developed some of their own concepts about micro-aggressions, and one of
my favourites is micro-invalidations. I learnt that from the school. I never thought of that
before. I think it's a fantastic term of micro-invalidations, which is I think what young
people are doing to each other a lot of time, but they came up with a word for it or they
found the word. I thank them for teaching it to me.
They then did similar sessions for Year 8 students in October 2025. November '25, they
did programs for their Year 9 students. They brought us back again into the school late
2025, and I could feel an absolute difference in school culture a year later, and I guess one
of the most pleasing pieces of that case study is, in May 2026, I visited the school and
I bumped into one of the school leaders, and she said, "I just want you to know that in
2026 we have had no incidents". So in 2025 and 2024, they had a lot of incidents, and
from February to May 2026, there were no incidents of antisemitism, no incidents of
racism within that school.
So I think that's a great example of what the school partnerships can enable a school to do
with a very small amount, a small investment from the government through us of $10,000
in a school that is obviously committed. And I'm sure the school used more time than we
paid for, but it was a great result.
COMMISSIONER: Are you able to tell us just one or more examples of the antisemitic
so-called jokes that had been circulating before?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Yes. One example in that school was a child being called a gas
inhaler. And they thought that was funny. Also at that school was a child being pushed
into a narrow space and being sprayed with deodorant and - to evoke the gas chambers.
Those are just two examples. I should say that in addition to the antisemitic examples, one
of the other examples that we heard at the school was the use of the word "slave" to refer
to Chinese students. Apparently that's a thing on gaming sites. I don't understand it, but
that's what they told us.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Rabbi, you have reflected at paragraph 40 of your statement that
some schools with the most need are the ones that end up receiving the least support.
Perhaps it's self-evident, but would you like to touch on why that creates difficulties?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Yes, so there are two types of problems with that. One is that
some schools, particularly schools in wealthier areas, have got volunteers who can write
some very persuasive applications that have very little connection to reality or are very
strong articulation of their case, where other schools that are struggling, where there's more
sort of lower on the spectrum of economic advantage, there's a greater pressure on schools,
and it's harder for them to articulate their need. I mean, one of the things that we try to

kind of level the playing field is that it's more of a conversation. So rather than getting
schools to write us fancy applications, Dr Beau or others on the team will have
a conversation with the schools, so we try and write that. But I think structurally it's
something to think about, the ways in which schools are able to articulate concerns and
that differential between schools.
MS PHILLIPS: You have also noted in your statement that a challenge that can arise is
perceptions around the purpose and appropriate audience for intercultural understanding
programs. Can you respond to why the Together for Humanity programs ought to be
directed to schools who might not have a diverse or intercultural community?
RABBI KASTEL AM: Absolutely. One of the well-intentioned but most irritating things
I hear in my work is a sense of looking at this purely from the perspective of the wellbeing
of victims and a sense that some of our children might be offended and therefore we need
to do something about this. I spoke to a senior leader within the Catholic system in
regional Australia who said that they were getting pushback in terms of dealing with
antisemitism because we have no Jewish students in our schools. It happens to be that in
that particular system, I have encountered two families of Jewish students, one of which
had a terrible time. But that's beside the point that I want to make.
The point I want to make is that hatred doesn't just harm the victim. Hatred harms the
hater. It's a toxic poison in the heart of people to see others as less than oneself or see one
as reduced to an "other" worthy of hatred. So when we look at addressing racism,
antisemitism, anti-Aboriginal prejudice or Islamophobia, whichever kind of hatred, and
think of it only in terms of the wellbeing of victims, that means that in schools where those
particular communities are not represented, that kind of hatred, misrepresentation goes
unchecked, goes unaddressed.
So if we are going to have social cohesion in Australia, if we are going to come together as
a country, if we are going to honour a social contract, it means all of us need to be part of
this, not just the schools with the Jewish students, for example.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Hu-Jia, can I come back to you on the topic of evaluation and
feedback for Together for Humanity's programs. At paragraph 22 of your statement, you
